title: Classical Physics 1
body:
Classical Physics 1 covers Newtonian mechanics, which answers one question: given the forces acting on an
object, where will it be later. The course builds the answer in three layers, and each layer is
a different way of avoiding work the previous one made expensive.

The first layer is kinematics, describing motion with position, velocity and acceleration
without asking what causes it. The second is dynamics, where [[Newton's Laws]] connect
force to acceleration, so the cause of the motion enters the calculation. The third is the
conservation laws, where [[Conservation of Energy]] and
[[Linear Momentum|momentum]] answer questions about the start and the end of a process
without tracking anything in between. Reaching for a conservation law when the details do not
matter is the judgement the course is really teaching.

It runs alongside [[CALCULUS 1]] and uses it constantly. Velocity is the [[Derivative]] of
position, acceleration is the derivative of velocity, and work is an [[Integral]] of force. The
course also assumes [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]'s [[Vector]], since force and velocity have
direction and adding them means adding components.

## Topics

### Vectors

A scalar has a magnitude alone, such as mass or time. A [[Vector]] has a magnitude and a
direction, which covers displacement, velocity, acceleration and force. Adding two vectors
means adding them component by component, and [[Vector Components]] covers the resolution
that makes that possible:

```
a vector of magnitude 20 at 30° above the horizontal

  x component:  20 cos 30° = 17.32
  y component:  20 sin 30° = 10.00
```

Once resolved, the two directions are independent and are solved as two separate
one-dimensional problems, which is the single technique the whole two-dimensional half of the
course runs on.

### Describing motion

[[Kinematics]] defines the three quantities and the relationships between them. Displacement is
the change in position, a vector from start to finish, which differs from distance travelled
whenever the path is not straight. Velocity is the rate of change of displacement and
acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so each is the [[Derivative]] of the one before
it.

[[Uniformly Accelerated Motion]] is the case where acceleration is constant, which
gives four equations relating the five quantities. Each equation omits one variable, so
choosing one means asking which quantity is neither known nor wanted:

```
v = v₀ + at                     omits displacement
Δx = v₀t + ½at²                 omits final velocity
v² = v₀² + 2aΔx                 omits time
Δx = ½(v₀ + v)t                 omits acceleration
```

### Motion in two dimensions

[[Projectile Motion]] is the standard application, and it works because the horizontal and
vertical components are independent. Gravity acts downward alone, so horizontal velocity stays
constant while vertical velocity changes at $9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.

```
launched at 20 m/s, 30° above horizontal

  vₓ = 17.32 m/s, constant           v_y = 10.0 m/s initially
  time to fall back:  2v_y/g = 2.04 s
  range:  17.32 × 2.04 = 35.3 m
  peak:   v_y²/2g = 5.1 m
```

A ball dropped and a ball fired horizontally from the same height hit the ground at the same
moment, which is the consequence worth remembering, and it follows from the independence of the
components, with nothing about the projectiles entering into it.

[[Uniform Circular Motion]] covers travel at constant speed around a circle, which is
accelerated motion because the direction of the velocity changes continuously. The acceleration
points at the centre and has magnitude $a = v^2/r$, so a car at 10 m/s on a 5 metre radius
experiences $20\ \text{m/s}^2$. Nothing supplies that acceleration on its own, which is why a
real turn requires friction or tension.

### Forces

[[Newton's Laws]] connect force to motion in three statements. An object keeps its
velocity until a net force changes it. The net force equals mass times acceleration, $\sum
\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}$, which is the equation the course solves over and over. Every force
is one half of a pair, so pushing on something means being pushed back equally.

A [[Free-Body Diagram]] is how a problem gets set up. Draw the object as a point, draw
every force acting on it as an arrow, resolve into components, and write $\sum F = ma$ per
direction. Most errors in the course are diagram errors, and the two most common are including
a force the object exerts on something else, and inventing a forward force on an object that is
coasting.

Three forces appear constantly. [[Friction]] opposes sliding, with magnitude $\mu N$, so a 10
kg block with $\mu = 0.3$ on a level surface needs $0.3 \times 10 \times 9.8 = 29.4$ N before
it moves. [[Tension]] is the pull transmitted along a rope, identical at both ends for an ideal
rope. The [[Normal Force]] is the surface pushing back perpendicular to itself, and it
equals the weight only when the surface is level and nothing else pushes vertically.

### Work and energy

The energy layer trades force and time for a scalar bookkeeping that ignores the path taken.

[[Work]] is force times displacement along the direction of the force, $W = Fd\cos\theta$, so a
20 N force over 5 metres in line with the motion does 100 J. A force perpendicular to the
motion does no work at all, which is why carrying a box across a room costs nothing in this
accounting and why the tension in a circular orbit changes no energy.

[[Kinetic Energy]] is $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, so a 10 kg object at 5 m/s carries 125 J. The
[[Work-Energy Theorem]] connects the two: the net work done on an object equals its change
in kinetic energy, which converts a force problem into an arithmetic problem whenever the
question asks only about speed.

[[Potential Energy]] is stored by position, $mgh$ for gravity near the surface and
$\frac{1}{2}kx^2$ for a spring. [[Conservation of Energy]] states that the total
stays constant when only conservative forces act:

```
dropped from 5 m:   mgh = ½mv²      the mass cancels
                    v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 5) = 9.9 m/s
```

That answer required no force, no time and no knowledge of the path, which is the whole
argument for the method. A ball rolling down any frictionless ramp of that height arrives at
the same speed.

### Momentum

[[Linear Momentum]] is $\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}$, and it is conserved for any system with
no external force, whatever happens inside it. [[Impulse]] is the change in momentum, equal to
force times the time it acts, which is why a longer collision at the same momentum change means
a smaller force and why airbags and crumple zones work.

[[Collisions]] is where the two conservation laws separate. Momentum is conserved in every
collision. Kinetic energy is conserved only in an elastic one:

```
2 kg at 3 m/s strikes 1 kg at rest, and they stick together

momentum:  (2)(3) + 0 = 6 = (3)v      so v = 2 m/s
KE before: ½(2)(3²) = 9 J
KE after:  ½(3)(2²) = 6 J             3 J went into deformation and heat
```

Momentum still balances while energy does not, which is what perfectly inelastic means. In an
elastic collision between equal masses with one at rest, the velocities are exchanged
completely, which is the result the lab demonstrates with air-track gliders.

### The laboratory

[[Measurement Uncertainty]] is what the lab component adds. Every measurement has a range,
uncertainties propagate through a calculation by rules that depend on the operation, and a
result quoted to more digits than the measurement supports is claiming precision that does not
exist. Comparing a measured value against a predicted one means asking whether the two ranges
overlap, which is the same question [[Hypothesis Testing]] asks in [[STATISTICS]] with a
probability attached.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 1]] supplies the machinery. Velocity is the [[Derivative]] of
  position and acceleration is the derivative of velocity, the kinematic equations are what
  integrating a constant acceleration produces, and [[Work]] is an [[Integral]] of force over
  distance.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] supplies the [[Vector]] and the [[Dot Product]], which is
  what $W = Fd\cos\theta$ is.
- [[STATISTICS]] supplies the treatment of [[Measurement Uncertainty]], where
  [[Variance]] and the [[Normal Distribution]] describe repeated measurements of one quantity.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] generalises the conservative force. A force that is the
  gradient of a potential is a [[Conservative Vector Field]], path independence is why
  [[Conservation of Energy]] works, and a non-conservative force is one with non-zero
  [[Curl]].
- [[THE UNIVERSE AT LARGE]] applies the same mechanics at astronomical scale,
  where orbital motion is [[Uniform Circular Motion]] with gravity supplying the centre-seeking
  force, and hydrostatic balance inside a star is a force diagram.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] measures [[Voltage]] and [[Current]] with the same
  uncertainty discipline the lab teaches.
